claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles is governed by the relative atomic diffusion rates of the constituent elements during synthesis.
Sufficiently similar diffusion rates among all noble metal components lead to homogeneous alloying.
Large disparities in constituent diffusion rates lead to phase separation, elemental segregation, or uncontrolled morphology.
Similar diffusion rates allow constituent atoms to mix efficiently at the nanoscale.
Efficient nanoscale mixing promotes homogeneous alloy formation.
Efficient nanoscale mixing promotes high surface-atom exposure.
When diffusion rates differ greatly, faster-diffusing elements segregate or form separate phases.
Systems with matched diffusion rates will yield homogeneous HEA nanoparticles with uniform composition.
Systems with matched diffusion rates will yield high surface-atom exposure.
Systems with mismatched diffusion rates will exhibit phase separation, elemental segregation, or non-uniform morphology.
Systems with mismatched diffusion rates will have reduced surface-atom exposure.
A composition with closely matched noble-metal diffusion rates yields homogeneous alloy nanoparticles under the stated baseline protocol.
The proposed diffusion-rate mechanism applies to noble metal–based HEA nanoparticle systems containing at least five elements and made by scalable protocols.
The mechanism does not apply when non-noble metals dominate the system.
Surfactants or templates can override diffusion-driven mixing.
Direct quantitative comparison of all constituent diffusion rates under synthesis-specific conditions may be difficult.
Precursor chemistry and nucleation kinetics may also influence HEA nanoparticle formation.
Obtaining homogeneous, high-surface-exposure nanoparticles from the widely mismatched system at a level comparable to the matched system would falsify the hypothesis.
